prompt: In the model this section uses to derive the ideal gas law, what forces do the gas particles exert on each other?

choices.text: None; they feel a force only when they hit a wall
A weak attraction that acts at all distances
choices.why: That describes a real gas. In an ideal gas the particles don't interact at all; the only forces come from collisions with the walls.

choices.text: A strong repulsion whenever two of them touch
choices.why: The model gives the particles no interactions, so they don't repel each other either. The only forces arise when a particle hits a wall.

choices.text: A force that keeps them all moving at one speed
choices.why: No force is needed to keep a particle moving. With no forces between particles, each one simply keeps its own speed until it hits a wall.

explanation: Ideal gases have no interactions between the particles, so the particles exert no forces on each other. A particle feels a force only when it collides with a wall of the container, and those collisions produce the pressure.

prompt: A particle moving with velocity v_x along x collides elastically with a wall perpendicular to x. What is the change in its velocity, Δv_x?

choices.text: −2v_x

choices.why: The speed is unchanged, but the velocity reverses from v_x to −v_x, so it changes by −v_x − v_x = −2v_x.

choices.text: −v_x
choices.why: That change would leave the particle at rest. In an elastic collision the velocity reverses to −v_x, a change of −2v_x.

choices.text: +v_x
choices.why: The change is the final velocity minus the initial one: −v_x − v_x = −2v_x.

explanation: In an elastic collision the velocity just changes sign: v_x before, −v_x after. So Δv_x = −v_x − v_x = −2v_x, while the speed stays the same.

prompt: Between collisions with the walls, how does a particle of an ideal gas move?

choices.text: In a straight line at constant speed
Faster and faster as it nears a wall
choices.why: Nothing pulls it toward the wall. With no forces acting between collisions, its speed stays constant.

choices.text: More and more slowly, losing energy to other particles
choices.why: Ideal-gas particles don't interact, so nothing slows them down. Each one keeps a constant speed until it hits a wall.

choices.text: Along a path bent by its neighbors' attraction
choices.why: Ideal-gas particles don't attract each other. With no forces on it, a particle moves in a straight line at constant speed.

explanation: Since no forces act on a particle except when it hits a wall, it moves at constant speed. A wall collision only reverses the velocity component perpendicular to that wall.

prompt: What is the mechanical definition of pressure used in this section's derivation?

choices.text: The average force on a wall divided by its area
The average force on a wall times its area
choices.why: Multiplying by the area gives the wrong units. Pressure is force per unit area: P = ⟨F⟩/A.

choices.text: The number of times per second particles hit a wall
choices.why: The collision rate affects the pressure, but pressure itself is the average force divided by the wall's area, P = ⟨F⟩/A.

choices.text: The average kinetic energy of one particle
choices.why: Kinetic energy is linked to temperature; it isn't the definition of pressure. Pressure is the average force on a wall divided by the wall's area.

explanation: The mechanical definition is P = ⟨F⟩/A, the average force over area. For a cubic box of side a, the wall's area is A = a^2.

prompt: The derivation of the ideal gas law combines Newton's laws with one result taken from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. Which result is that?

choices.text: F_x = (m v_x^2)/a
choices.why: This force comes from Newton's second law and the time between wall collisions. The Maxwell–Boltzmann result is ⟨v_x^2⟩ = (k_B T)/m.
This comes from the geometry of the box: the particle travels 2a between hits on the same wall. The Maxwell–Boltzmann result is ⟨v_x^2⟩ = (k_B T)/m.

choices.text: P = (nRT)/V
choices.why: That is the final result, the ideal gas law itself. The input from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution is ⟨v_x^2⟩ = (k_B T)/m.

explanation: Newton's laws give P = (N m⟨v_x^2⟩)/(a^3). The Maxwell–Boltzmann result ⟨v_x^2⟩ = (k_B T)/m then turns this into P = (N k_B T)/V, since a^3 = V.

prompt: According to P = (N m⟨v_x^2⟩)/V, a heavier particle pushes harder on the wall at a given speed. At the same N, V and T, how does the pressure of a gas of heavy molecules compare with that of a gas of light molecules?

choices.text: It is the same
It is higher, in proportion to the mass
choices.why: Heavier molecules move more slowly: ⟨v_x^2⟩ = (k_B T)/m, so m⟨v_x^2⟩ = k_B T for any mass, and P = (N k_B T)/V.

choices.text: It is lower, because heavy molecules move slowly
choices.why: They do move more slowly, but each hit carries more momentum. The two effects cancel exactly, since m⟨v_x^2⟩ = k_B T.

choices.text: It depends on how strongly the molecules attract
choices.why: Ideal-gas molecules don't attract each other at all. Since m⟨v_x^2⟩ = k_B T for any mass, the pressure is the same.

explanation: With ⟨v_x^2⟩ = (k_B T)/m, the product m⟨v_x^2⟩ equals k_B T whatever the mass, so P = (N k_B T)/V. The pressure of an ideal gas depends only on N, V and T, not on what the molecules are.

prompt: The derivation ends with P = (N k_B T)/V and then writes this as nRT/V, where n = N/N_0 is the number of moles and N_0 is Avogadro's number. For the two forms to agree, how must R be related to k_B?

choices.text: R = N_0 k_B
R = k_B/N_0
choices.why: Then nRT would equal N k_B T divided by N_0^2. Since N = nN_0, matching N k_B to nR requires R = N_0 k_B.

choices.text: R = k_B
choices.why: R and k_B differ by Avogadro's number: R is the constant per mole and k_B the constant per molecule, so R = N_0 k_B.

choices.text: R = N k_B
choices.why: R is a constant; it can't depend on how many particles the sample holds. Since N = nN_0, N k_B = nR gives R = N_0 k_B.

explanation: With N = nN_0, N k_B T = n(N_0 k_B)T, so the two forms agree when R = N_0 k_B. R is the gas constant per mole; k_B is the same constant per molecule.

prompt: A particle in a cubic box of side a = 0.10 m moves along x with v_x = 500 m/s, bouncing elastically between the walls at x = 0 and x = a. To hit the wall at x = 0 again it must travel 2a, so the time between these hits is Δt = (2a)/(v_x). What is Δt, in seconds? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-4.)
explanation: Δt = (2 × 0.10 m)/(500 m/s) = 0.20/500 s = 4.0 × 10^−4 s. The particle goes to the far wall and back before it strikes the wall at x = 0 again.

prompt: In the derivation, one particle bouncing between two walls a distance a apart exerts an average force F_x = (m v_x^2)/a on each wall. What is F_x, in newtons, for m = 5.0 × 10^−26 kg, v_x = 400 m/s and a = 0.20 m? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e-20.)
explanation: v_x^2 = 400^2 m^2/s^2 = 1.6 × 10^5 m^2/s^2, so F_x = 5.0 × 10^−26 × 1.6 × 10^5/0.20 N = 4.0 × 10^−20 N. One molecule pushes very weakly; the pressure comes from the enormous number of them.

prompt: The derivation uses ⟨v_x^2⟩ = (k_B T)/m from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. Using k_B = 1.38 × 10^−23 J/K, what is ⟨v_x^2⟩, in m^2/s^2, for N2 molecules (m = 4.60 × 10^−26 kg) at T = 300 K? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e4.)
explanation: k_B T = 1.38 × 10^−23 J/K × 300 K = 4.14 × 10^−21 J, so ⟨v_x^2⟩ = 4.14 × 10^−21/4.60 × 10^−26 m^2/s^2 = 9.00 × 10^4 m^2/s^2. Its square root, 300 m/s, is a typical speed along one direction.

prompt: A 1.00 L box (V = 1.00 × 10^−3 m^3) holds N = 2.50 × 10^22 gas molecules at T = 300 K. Using P = (N k_B T)/V with k_B = 1.38 × 10^−23 J/K, what is the pressure, in Pa? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e5.)
What is an equation of state?

choices.text: A relation among P, V and T that describes a substance's state
An equation that gives how fast a gas changes from one state to another
choices.why: An equation of state has no time or rate in it. It relates variables such as P, V and T under given conditions.

choices.text: An equation that is valid only for gases with no interactions
choices.why: PV = nRT is one equation of state, but real gases have others, such as the van der Waals equation. Any relation among P, V and T that describes the state counts.

choices.text: A rule that lists which phases a substance has at each temperature
choices.why: That would be a phase diagram, not an equation of state. An equation of state relates variables such as P, V and T under a given set of conditions.

explanation: An equation of state is a relation between variables, such as P, V and T, that describes the state of matter under a set of given physical conditions. The ideal gas law is one example.

prompt: When a gas particle strikes a wall, it exerts a force F_x on the wall. What force does the wall exert on the particle?

choices.text: −F_x, equal in size and opposite in direction
Zero, because the wall doesn't move
choices.why: A wall can push without moving. By Newton's third law it pushes back on the particle with −F_x, and that force is what reverses the particle's velocity.

choices.text: +F_x, in the same direction as the particle's push
choices.why: Action and reaction point in opposite directions. The wall pushes back with −F_x, which is what turns the particle around.

choices.text: −2F_x, twice as large as the particle's push
choices.why: The two forces are exactly equal in size. By Newton's third law the wall exerts −F_x, equal and opposite to the particle's push.

explanation: Since every action has an equal and opposite reaction, the wall exerts a force −F_x on the particle. Through Newton's second law, this force reverses the particle's velocity component v_x.

prompt: Isotherms are curves of P against V at a fixed temperature. On a P–V graph of ideal-gas isotherms for the same amount of gas, how does the isotherm for a higher temperature compare with one for a lower temperature?

choices.text: It lies above it, with a higher P at every V
It lies below it, with a lower P at every V
choices.why: From P = nRT/V, raising T raises P at any fixed V, so the hotter isotherm lies above.

choices.text: The two curves cross at one particular volume
choices.why: Ideal-gas isotherms never cross: at any V the pressure is proportional to T, so the hotter one is always higher.

choices.text: It is a straight line instead of a curve
choices.why: Every ideal-gas isotherm has the same shape, P ∝ 1/V. A higher T just raises the curve to a higher P at every V.

explanation: For an ideal gas, P = nRT/V. At a given V the pressure is proportional to T, so isotherms for higher temperatures lie above those for lower ones and never cross them.

prompt: Ideal-gas isochores are straight lines of P against T, each at a fixed molar density ρ. Since P = ρRT, which isochore is the steepest?

choices.text: The one with the highest density
The one with the lowest density
choices.why: The slope of P against T is ρR, so a lower density gives a shallower line.

choices.text: None; they all have the same slope
choices.why: The slope of P = ρRT plotted against T is ρR, so lines for different densities have different slopes.

choices.text: The one at the highest temperature
choices.why: Each isochore covers a range of temperatures; it is labeled by its density. Its slope, ρR, is largest for the highest density.

explanation: Along an isochore ρ is fixed, so P = ρRT is a straight line through the origin with slope ρR. The higher the density, the steeper the line.

prompt: A sealed sample of an ideal gas is heated at fixed volume, so it moves along an isochore, P = ρRT with ρ constant. If its pressure is 2.00 bar at 300 K, what is its pressure at 450 K, in bar?
explanation: With ρ and R fixed, P is proportional to T: P = 2.00 bar × 450/300 = 3.00 bar. Plotted against T, each isochore is a straight line through the origin.

prompt: Why can't an ideal gas condense into a liquid, however much it is cooled or compressed?

choices.text: Its particles have no interactions at all
Its collisions with the walls are elastic
choices.why: Elastic wall collisions don't prevent condensation. A gas-to-liquid transition can be modeled only if the particles interact, and ideal-gas particles don't.

choices.text: It is always above its boiling point
choices.why: An ideal gas can be at any temperature. It can't condense because its particles have no interactions to hold a liquid together.

choices.text: Its particles take up no volume
choices.why: Particle size isn't what stops condensation. A gas-to-liquid transition can be modeled only if the particles interact, and ideal-gas particles don't.

explanation: An ideal gas can exist only as a gas; there is no ideal liquid. A phase transition from gas to liquid can be modeled only if the interactions between particles are properly accounted for.

prompt: What is the compressibility factor Z of a gas?

choices.text: Z = (PV)/(nRT)

choices.why: That is the compressibility, a different quantity. The compressibility factor is the ratio Z = (PV)/(nRT).

choices.text: Z = (nRT)/(PV)
choices.why: That is the reciprocal. The compressibility factor is Z = (PV)/(nRT), which equals 1 for an ideal gas.

choices.text: Z = PV − nRT
choices.why: A difference would have units of energy. Z is the ratio (PV)/(nRT), a pure number equal to 1 for an ideal gas.

explanation: Rearranging PV = nRT gives (PV)/(nRT) = 1. This ratio is the compressibility factor Z; for a real gas, how far Z is from 1 measures how far the gas deviates from ideal behavior.

prompt: An ideal gas at a fixed temperature is compressed by raising its pressure. What happens to its compressibility factor Z?

choices.text: It stays exactly 1
It rises above 1
choices.why: As P rises, V falls in proportion, so PV stays equal to nRT and Z stays 1.

choices.text: It falls below 1
choices.why: Real gases can show Z below 1, but in an ideal gas V falls in proportion to the rise in P, so Z stays 1.

choices.text: It rises in proportion to P
choices.why: Z contains PV, not P alone. For an ideal gas, V shrinks as P grows, keeping PV = nRT and Z = 1.

explanation: In an ideal gas, compressing by increasing P makes the volume decrease just enough to keep Z = (PV)/(nRT) = 1. Only real gases show Z different from 1.

prompt: Measured Z values of real gases such as N2, CH4, H2 and CO2 differ from 1 at high pressures. What happens to Z for each of them as the pressure is lowered toward zero?

choices.text: It approaches 1
It approaches 0
choices.why: Z isn't proportional to P: as P falls, V grows. At low pressure each gas approaches ideal behavior, Z = 1.

choices.text: It keeps a different value for each gas
choices.why: At low enough pressures, and so low densities, every gas approaches ideal behavior, so all of them reach Z = 1.

choices.text: It grows without limit
choices.why: Z doesn't run away at low pressure. At sufficiently low pressures every gas approaches ideal-gas behavior, where Z = 1.

explanation: For sufficiently low pressures, and hence low densities, each gas approaches ideal-gas behavior, so its Z approaches 1. That is the sense of this section's title: all dilute gases behave ideally.

prompt: A real gas has Z = 0.80 at some pressure and temperature. Since Z = (PV̄)/(RT), how does its molar volume compare with that of an ideal gas at the same P and T?

choices.text: It is smaller, 0.80 times the ideal value
It is larger, 1.25 times the ideal value
choices.why: V̄ = (ZRT)/P, and the ideal gas has Z = 1. With Z = 0.80 the molar volume is 0.80 times the ideal value, so it is smaller.

choices.text: It is the same, since P and T are the same
choices.why: At the same P and T, V̄ is proportional to Z. With Z = 0.80, V̄ is 0.80 times the ideal value.

choices.text: It is smaller, 0.64 times the ideal value
choices.why: V̄ is proportional to Z itself, not to Z^2. With Z = 0.80 the molar volume is 0.80 times the ideal value.

explanation: At fixed P and T, V̄ = (ZRT)/P, and an ideal gas has Z = 1. So Z = 0.80 means the gas takes up 0.80 times the ideal molar volume; how far Z is from 1 measures the deviation from ideal behavior.

prompt: A gas at T = 300 K and P = 40.0 bar has a molar density ρ = 2.00 mol/L. Using the intensive form Z = P/(ρRT) with R = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K), what is its compressibility factor? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: ρRT = 2.00 × 0.08314 × 300 bar = 49.88 bar, so Z = 40.0/49.88 = 0.802. An ideal gas at this density and temperature would exert 49.88 bar; a Z this far below 1 shows a noticeable deviation from ideal behavior.

prompt: In thermodynamics, what makes up the thermodynamic universe?

choices.text: The system, its surroundings and the boundary
The system and its boundary, but not the surroundings
choices.why: The surroundings belong to it too. The thermodynamic universe is the system, its surroundings and the boundary between them.

choices.text: Only the surroundings outside the system
choices.why: The system belongs to it as well. Together, the system, its surroundings and the boundary make up the thermodynamic universe.

choices.text: The system alone, once it is sealed
choices.why: A sealed system is still only one part. The thermodynamic universe is the system plus its surroundings plus the boundary between them.

explanation: Thermodynamics divides the universe into a system and its surroundings, with a boundary between them. The unity of all three is the thermodynamic universe.

prompt: A system is made larger so that both N and V grow while the ratio N/V stays constant. What is an extensive property?

choices.text: One that increases as the system grows
One that stays the same as the system grows
choices.why: That is an intensive property, such as temperature or pressure. An extensive property, such as volume, increases as the system grows.

choices.text: One that depends only on the temperature
choices.why: The test is how a property scales with the size of the system. An extensive property increases as the system grows; an intensive one stays the same.

choices.text: One that can be measured only at the boundary
choices.why: Where it is measured doesn't matter. An extensive property is one that increases as the system grows with N/V held constant.

explanation: When a system grows with N/V held constant, an extensive property (such as N, n, V, mass or energy) increases, and an intensive property (such as P, T or density) stays the same.

prompt: Which of these properties is extensive?

choices.text: Free energy
Temperature
choices.why: Temperature stays the same when the system grows with N/V fixed, so it is intensive. Free energy grows with the system.

choices.text: Pressure
choices.why: Pressure doesn't change when the system grows with N/V fixed, so it is intensive. Free energy grows with the system.

choices.text: Molar heat capacity
choices.why: A molar quantity is per mole, so it doesn't change as the system grows; the section lists it as intensive. Free energy grows with the system.

explanation: The section lists N, n, V, mass, energy and free energy as extensive, and pressure, density, molar heat capacity and temperature as intensive.

prompt: Two identical samples of a gas, each at 300 K and 1 bar, are combined into one system with twice the amount of gas and twice the volume. What is the temperature of the combined system?

choices.why: Temperatures don't add. T is intensive: it stays the same when the system grows with N/V fixed.
The temperature isn't shared out between the two halves. T is intensive, so the combined system stays at 300 K.

choices.text: It can't be known without the amount of gas
choices.why: T is intensive: it doesn't depend on the size of the system, so the combined system is still at 300 K.

explanation: Doubling both n and V keeps N/V fixed, which is exactly the growth that separates extensive from intensive properties. Temperature, like pressure, is intensive and stays at 300 K, while V, n and the energy double.

prompt: In the intensive form of the ideal gas law, P = ρRT, what does ρ stand for?

choices.text: The molar density, n/V
The number density, N/V
choices.why: With the number of particles per volume, the law would read P = ρk_B T. With R in it, ρ must be the moles per volume, n/V.

choices.text: The mass density, m/V
choices.why: With mass per volume, ρRT wouldn't have units of pressure. With R in it, ρ is the molar density, n/V.

choices.text: The molar volume, V/n
choices.why: That is V̄, the reciprocal of ρ; the law in terms of it is PV̄ = RT. ρ is the molar density, n/V.

explanation: ρ = n/V is the molar density and V̄ = V/n is the molar volume. Both are intensive, so P = ρRT and PV̄ = RT are intensive forms of PV = nRT.

prompt: Why is PV̄ = RT called an intensive form of the ideal gas law, while PV = nRT is not?

choices.text: None of P, V̄ and T grows with the system
It holds only for exactly one mole of gas
choices.why: V̄ = V/n is a molar quantity, so the form holds for any amount. It is intensive because P, V̄ and T don't depend on the system's size.

choices.text: It applies only to small samples of gas
choices.why: Size doesn't matter. Each quantity in it (P, V̄ and T) stays the same as the system grows, which is what makes it intensive.

choices.text: It leaves out the volume, which is extensive
choices.why: It doesn't leave the volume out; it uses the volume per mole, V/n. Since V̄, P and T all stay the same as the system grows, the form is intensive.

explanation: PV = nRT contains V and n, which grow with the system. PV̄ = RT uses only P, T and the molar volume V̄ = V/n, which all stay the same when the system grows, so it is written in intensive form.

prompt: Using the intensive form PV̄ = RT with R = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K), what is the molar volume V̄ of an ideal gas at T = 273.15 K and P = 1.000 bar, in L/mol? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: V̄ = RT/P = 0.08314 × 273.15/1.000 L/mol = 22.71 L/mol. Like P and T, V̄ is intensive: it is the same for any amount of the gas.
